title: Right Effort
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of balance and pacing in sustaining a spiritual practice, highlighting how finding a sense of inner equilibrium allows one to approach their path with clarity and motivation. This balance is not about achieving perfection, but rather about cultivating patience, stamina, and joy in one's daily life and spiritual practice. By recognizing the interconnectedness of aspiration, commitment, inspiration, and joy/ease/love, individuals can sustain right effort and momentum, even in the face of challenges and obstacles.

sentences.text: That was the first major accomplishment.
Good evening, everyone.
Can you hear me okay, everybody?
You guys on Zoom?
I think you can.
Okay.
So this evening, I thought I would continue, taking up where John left off last week on Right Effort.
I'm going to talk a little bit more about that.
Right Effort is the sixth of the Noble Eightfold Path, as we talked about last week.
As John described last week, it's an internal direction—it's a skillful ability to select a skillful path and an inner ability to sustain practice.
Throughout my journey to Tassajara Zen Center and back, I've been aware of some factors needed for Right Effort.
The trip itself and the Dharma sharing discussions that we had while we were there really set the stage for me to explore this a little bit more.
The combination really allowed me to take a deeper look into the ingredients that give and sustain energy and the factors that may be missing sometimes in my daily life at one time or another.
But first, I want to give you a little bit of background about the trip to Tassajara and its connection with Right Effort.
As many of you know, I just recently returned from there, and it was really the realization of a lifelong dream.
My desire to go to Tassajara began long ago, before I knew I was Buddhist.
That came from my deep calling, nonetheless; just an inkling of the place placed a seed in me as it drifted into my realm way back in the seventies in Boulder.
I got the Tassajara bread book, and I love the meal chant in the front, and I still remember it to this day.
So it really remained with me all over all of those years, and then many years later I found myself practicing here.
It's just so amazing to me in the lineage of Shinryu Suzuki Roshi, who founded Tassajara Zen Center.
As I moved into this practice, however, I really felt myself letting go of that dream of Tassajara with more limited ambulatory skills than ever before and using the walker rollator.

I knew from pictures and stories that Tassajara was not the most accessible place in the world to get around, with uneven dirt and rock paths, lots of steps, lots of ups and downs, deep in the heart of the Ventana wilderness in California.
I heard stories from Kanho Chris and others of the beautiful but rigorous stays there during their three-month monastic trainings.
I could only imagine what they experienced there with the familiar twinge of longing and jealousy because I listened to the remembrances, but resolute in the idea that it would not happen for me.
And then it happened.

I saw this announcement that Gil Fronsdale, who's a really well-known, very beloved teacher in the Theravadan tradition, was offering a three-week intensive there this summer—actually, I think it's happening right now.
I mentioned it to Chris, wouldn't that be so incredible?
Instead of replying, "Yes, it would be so great," she offered, "You can do it."
"What?"
"You always told me that I couldn't do it," she replied.
"Three months would be too much, but you could do three weeks."
It just like opened up this possibility in my mind.
I thought, could I do it?
She really encouraged me to reach out and find out if that could work for me.
Meanwhile, in the many years as a practitioner, though, even though I knew about Tassajara for years and years and years before that, I didn't want to go as a guest during guest season.
I wanted to go as a Zen student; I wanted to go as a practitioner.
So meanwhile, I emailed my teacher, Ryushin Andrea Thatch, who many of you know was a teacher here for some years.
Anyway, I told her about my lifelong dream and the possibility.
When I told her that, she said, "In fact, I am taking a cohort of people there to Tassajara for this five-day Dharma study week."
I couldn't believe it.
I felt that it would be very likely that I may get a slot in their spot.
I was really determined that I could do it; I could somehow make it work because the chance to not only go to Tassajara but to go and practice with my teacher and her sangha is just like what a gift.
So, it began the process of planning and preparing, which took a different kind of energy.

I thought of driving myself down to California by myself, driving myself and others to Tassajara, the moment by moment maneuvering around the grounds, even imagining the strong heat, the extreme heat took energy.
Could I do it?
I was aware of my fretting energy at that point, too.
Actually, I don't have this in my notes, but I was thinking about how it's such a balance when you're having to plan something in the future.
You have to plan it; you have to think about it.
But it's such a balance not to start like imagining and fretting over the hundred-degree heat or whatever.
So it was really an interesting process.
But I knew that that was the fretting energy; it was not the energy that was going to carry me to Tassajara.
So, I ultimately drew on the experience in that present moment as I was there.
I think that's true with everything we can fret and worry and plan on the future, but it's in that moment, if you're present in the moment, none of that is there.
So I thought that was really interesting.
I did find my way around.
It took a lot of ongoing physical energy, and I did continue to have energy for everything that was offered.
So, I was able to participate in all of the sessions, take part in the schedule, do my work practice, and all of those things.
What was most surprising was that I did this all with a much greater sense of ease than I had imagined.
So, yeah, I was savoring my moments there, and I had so much gratitude for being there.
During our time at Tassajara, my teacher Ryushin and her co-teacher Susan brought excerpts with them from Sojun Mel Weitsman, their teacher.
He recently passed away, as many of you know, a couple of years ago.
Those who are not familiar with Sojun Mel, he studied in the early years at Tassajara with Suzuki Roshi and helped build Tassajara.
He was the longtime abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center, and he gave Dharma transmission to both my teacher and Norman Fisher and many other people during his life at Berkeley Zen Center.
Sojun Mel lived at Tassajara here and there for many years.
When we were there, we were really paying homage not only to Suzuki Roshi but really to Sojun Mel as well, and felt his energy.
It was just so wonderful.
It was a really special gift to be able to use Sojun's excerpts.
That book is forthcoming, maybe in the fall; he was writing it in his last months of his life.
It's just a very special thing that they brought it.
In the midst of those teachings and my musings on my energy and the journey to Tassajara, I felt it was just such a wonderful combination.
But I want to share a few of the excerpts with you as we go along and see if these bring up thoughts of your own connected to right effort.

The first thing we read from Sojun's excerpts were these things: *When I was in high school, I ran the 100-yard dash with a burst of speed as fast as I could, while some ran the mile and others even did a marathon.
I couldn't understand how they had patience, much less the stamina to run that far.
In the Buddha Dharma, there's an example of three animals, the rabbit, the horse, and the elephant, kind of like the rabbit and the tortoise, I think.
The rabbit was the sprinter, hopping all over the place as fast as he could.
The horse was running around but a little bit more settled, but the wise elephant was very careful, taking slow and deliberate steps without being scattered and hasty.
And if careful, would live a long and wise and useful life.
So the elephant represents the Buddha Dharma.*
At that point, Rishi Nandia noted that the description of the elephant with its slow, methodical and never-ceasing steps was also Sojun Mel.
We agreed in this discussion that balance is an important factor for sustaining practice; slow and steady wins the race.
I have learned over many years about the balance, the importance of pacing.
When I swim, I'm an elephant.
Others always swim faster, but almost no one paces themselves enough to continue the full duration without stopping, as I am able to do.
Because of that, many years ago, I think I said this before in some talk, when I was walking without a walker, we were doing some hiking and my husband was just like, "It was such a gift."
He really taught me how to pace myself because I could never race up the hiking trails.
In Boulder, those trails are packed, so you're always kind of under pressure.
Torini just kept saying, "Slow down, just take, go slow enough so that you can sustain and not have to stop."
It was really a great thing for my overall life practice.
So Sojun Mel continued, "Establishing a rhythm is essential.
If the runner goes too fast, he gets tired too soon."
Then Mel continued, "If she doesn't have enough momentum, her energy leaks and is not renewed."
Right away, my teacher thought of a question: What gives momentum?
What is it that allows this momentum to continue?
I want to stop just for one second and allow you to think about that for your own life.
How do you sustain your practice?
For me, the thing that came to mind was aspiration.
Deep aspiration on this path sustains my practice.
This is what gives me energy at the deepest level to continue.
It is what gives me momentum so that this effort doesn't all leak out.
And that's what I feel like is an important factor in my right effort.
Sojun Mel went on to talk about dedication and commitment—a commitment to yourself.
You can't practice without commitment, he said.
He suggested going to your teacher and having them help with a commitment that's doable, so you're not slacking off but you're not taking on too much.
He was also talking about how it's really important in right effort to not go by how we feel, but to really rely on this commitment.
If we go by how we feel day to day, it could be, "I'm kind of tired today.
Oh, I deserve a special treat.
I don't know if I feel like driving up the lasanga meeting tonight.
Sometimes, I just need to relax."
We all have those thoughts, and depending on what we're doing, they all come up as either habit energies that we can push through or ones that stop us.
It's just really nice to be aware of that.
So he said, don't depend on your feelings, depend on your commitment.
I didn't know him personally, but from everything everyone's told me, I think that his strongest trait was commitment.
They say he never missed an early morning sit at the Berkeley Zen Center; he was always there.
I noticed when my commitment is strong, it's really easy to not get overcome by life's activities.
However, my journey to Tassajara was both my commitment and my aspiration that were so strong they couldn't be undone by the hesitation or fears or habit energies that came up.
So Sojun Mel also talked about Zazen as the touchstone to our practice, the center.
And then he interjected, "Lest we forget, the fruit of practice is compassion."
This is kind of an aside, but for me, this is what I am finding with Zazen and with practice.
Compassion isn't the goal of practice; it isn't something that you try to force yourself to have.
It's the fruit of practice.
It's the thing that naturally arises from our Zazen and from our practice.
He says that when we practice selflessly, there is no self to get tired, and this no self is continuously renewed.
I love this, and I think it's really true.
I think of my heroes who have devoted their entire lives to work for the benefit of all beings and who continue in the midst of incredibly harsh situations.
I always think, how do they continue?
It's this.
So this leads me right into the next factor that I'm thinking about contributing to right effort, which is inspiration.
Who inspires me and why?
How does that sustain right effort and give me momentum?
My teacher inspires me, as well as many other teachers in other forms than our ancient ancestral teachers, including the human being that was the Buddha.
One important observation in that is that wisdom, I think, arises from direct experience.
I can see that my teachers bend down the road and back, and it's that knowing of the truth.
Experience itself in our practice gives rise to insight and right view.
I also derive inspiration from great sutras.

I love the instruction in the teachings, for example, the Avatamsaka Sutra, which I'm enjoying right now, is filled with clear and beautiful instruction for those of us on the path of the Bodhisattva.
Like a child who sees and models the skills of a good parent, I gain energy from seeing that others can and do continue on this path as well, despite all obstacles; they help sustain my practice.

These factors not only contribute to right effort, but because the facets of the Noble Eightfold Path are all interrelated, I can also see how they sustain right intention, which leads to right action.
Maybe we'll be hearing about some of those other facets of the path in the weeks to come.
I'm also aware that other factors contribute to right effort, and these are joy and ease and love.
I also know that I cannot sustain energy for things that I try to force in some way.
I may be able to sprint for a while, but without an authentic heart, I'm going to burn out and it won't last long.

As I was writing, I thought of the characteristics that I've been talking about, and also realized that during the Shusso during the winter practice period, those that all gave me energy for the classes, for the talks, that whole journey too.
I really see that it was aspiration, inspiration, commitment, joy, ease, and love.
I didn't put this in there, but I was thinking that creativity is such a huge piece of being able to sustain right effort.
If you don't have a creative outlet, it's difficult; it's easy to burn out.
Long ago, I was in an internship, and I just remember these two very different parts of the internship.
One really, I just wilted; I was in a box and I couldn't get out.
The other one, this person that was leading it, she was a risk-taker and she was so free about letting me explore and do things on my own and have creativity.
I just blossomed after the previous one, and it was really amazing to me the difference.
I've been thinking about these factors needed for right effort and pondering that in relationship to my ongoing activities.
These activities require a variety of different amounts of effort, and they're certainly not of that intensity that allowed me to get all the way to Tassajara and back.

Activities such as daily life, my activities here, coming to the Sangha, showing up, taking care of my health, eating well, taking care of my house, devoting time to others—those are all things that require energy.
As John talked about in his talk last week, the idea is to help the unwholesome seeds return to the store consciousness and focus on watering the good seeds and making them grow.
In my routines, I sometimes forget, I ignore some of these factors that we've been exploring and how they really relate to my everyday life to certainly around my spiritual practice.
It's all spiritual practice, but I can see it's easier to reach it and touch it.

But being aware of this with each step is a never-ending thing, whether it's inner or outer, whether taking care of health or cleaning the house; they're all activities that contribute to peace and well-being.
I struggle with things.
For instance, I struggle with eating healthfully.
I have really strong habit energies around using food.
I enjoy food as a form of adventure; I use it as comfort and as a distraction and an escape.
A simple phrase that has been really helping me in the last few months in making choices and being more upfront in my mind is something I presented in one of the classes.
I gave some exercises suggested by Gil Fronsdale from his book entitled *Steps to Liberation: The Buddhist Eightfold Path*.
I think many of you are still going through those exercises, maybe.
This one is just really with me and it was so helpful in remembering to water the seeds that contribute to right effort.
It's this: *Nourish your inner life and instead of doing activities that bring pleasure, do things that bring satisfaction, meaning and happiness to your heart.
That is right effort.* The simple reminder has been really invaluable to me.
It speaks to me about living by vow and not by habit energies.
It speaks about energy that gives rise to the deepest sense of nourishment and joy.
It speaks not about choices that fulfill instant gratification or greediness or laziness.

It speaks about the energy that it took to get me to Tassajara and back: a deep aspiration, a deep calling, and an eventual letting go of frets and worries and having faith that right effort would give me what I needed.
I'd like to leave you with that, but I want us to get into some small groups now.
Maybe there's quite a few people; I think we could get into groups of four, and we'll spend, I don't know, fifteen minutes or something.
Maybe, how many are there?
Twenty.
Yeah, I guess groups of four.
I don't have a bell, but I'll make a sound in between each person.
So spend three or four minutes each talking about something.
Then if we have time, we'll come back and see if anybody has anything they want to share with the whole group.
I want you to think about these two questions that we've been talking about.
The first one, you can think about one or both or whatever you want to talk about, but they are: what are factors that sustain your own right effort?
And what are factors that cause your energy to leak?
I just kind of think about that for a few minutes.
If you want to get into groups of four, that would be great.
Chris, do you know how to do a breakout room for Scott and Edie?
Would you guys like that we're going to try to put you in a room?
I don't know how to do it.
Hold on to that, please.
I'm going to stop recording, too.
Oh, yes.
Thank you.
You can just go around, start with one person.
